newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr mortgage rates fall in week ending Aug 1.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr mortgage rates fall in week ending Aug 1.

text.p: Average commitment rates on U.S. 30- and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages fell during the week ending August 1 to their lowest levels in more than a year, Freddie Mac said Thursday.

Thirty-year mortgages in the week fell to an average 7.36 percent from 7.43 percent last week. Fifteen-year mortgages fell to an average 6.90 percent from 6.98 percent last week, Freddie Mac reported.

The 30-year mortgage rate was at its lowest level since the week ended February 23, 1996, when it was at 7.32 percent. The 15-year rate was at its lowest level since the week ended March 8, 1996, when it hit 6.96 percent.
One-year adjustable rate mortgages were also down, falling to 5.49 percent in the week from 5.54 percent last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.23 percent, the 15-year 7.75 percent and the ARM 5.98 percent.

The fall in interest rates can be attributed to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony last week that growth is slowing, as well as to the tentative budget accord reached by Democrats and Republicans, Freddie Mac chief economist Robert Van Order said.

"Interest rates dropped this week partly in response to Fed Chairman Greenspan's optimistic remarks of last week, but also as a result of news of the upcoming federal budget agreement,"Van Order said.
"The budget agreement news may well carry over into next week, bringing us interest rates that are even more affordable than they are now."
Fees and points charged by lenders for 30-year and 15-year loans were unchanged from last week at an average 1.7 percent. ARM loans remained unchanged at 1.4 percent in the August 1 week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
